claim: When sampling is limiting, the efficient coding principle leads to a 'variance is salience' hypothesis.
source: Previously, in Hermundstad et al., 2014, we showed that when sampling is limiting, the efficient coding principle leads to a 'variance is salience' hypothesis
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hermundstad et al., 2014) that established this theoretical relationship.

claim: The 'variance is salience' hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to binary image statistics.
source: Previously, in Hermundstad et al., 2014, we showed that when sampling is limiting, the efficient coding principle leads to a 'variance is salience' hypothesis, and that this hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to binary image statistics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hermundstad et al., 2014) that demonstrated this relationship experimentally.

claim: The 'variance is salience' hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to a large set of grayscale image statistics at a striking level of detail.
source: Here, using extensive new psychophysical data and image analysis, we show that this hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to a large set of grayscale image statistics at a striking level of detail
evidence: This claim is supported by the new psychophysical data and image analysis presented in this manuscript.

claim: A 66-dimensional space of local grayscale light-intensity correlations can be defined.
source: We define a 66-dimensional space of local grayscale light-intensity correlations
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the mathematical construction described in the manuscript.

claim: The 'variance is salience' hypothesis predicts that two-point correlations are most salient.
source: The 'variance is salience' hypothesis predicts that two-point correlations are most salient
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the efficient coding framework applied to the texture space.

claim: Correlations beyond second order are not salient.
source: As predicted, correlations beyond second order are not salient
evidence: This claim is supported by the psychophysical measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Predicted thresholds for over 300 second-order correlations match psychophysical thresholds closely with median fractional error <0.13.
source: predicted thresholds for over 300 second-order correlations match psychophysical thresholds closely (median fractional error <0.13)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements.

claim: Neural circuits in the periphery of the visual system use limited resources efficiently to represent sensory information by adapting to the statistical structure of the environment.
source: Neural circuits in the periphery of the visual (Laughlin, 1981; Atick and Redlich, 1990; van Hateren, 1992; Fairhall et al., 2001; Ratliff et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2009; Borghuis et al., 2008; Garrigan et al., 2010; Kuang et al., 2012), auditory (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001; Lewicki, 2002; Smith and Lewicki, 2006; Carlson et al., 2012), and perhaps also olfactory (Teşileanu et al., 2019) systems use limited resources efficiently to represent sensory information by adapting to the statistical structure of the environment (Sterling and Laughlin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work across different sensory modalities.

claim: Efficient coding might occur in the primary visual cortex.
source: There is some evidence that this sort of efficient coding might also occur more centrally, in the primary visual cortex (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Bell and Sejnowski, 1997; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; van Hateren and van der Schaaf, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work, though the claim is qualified as having 'some evidence'.

claim: Efficient coding might occur in the entorhinal cortex.
source: There is some evidence that this sort of efficient coding might also occur more centrally, in the primary visual cortex (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Bell and Sejnowski, 1997; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; van Hateren and van der Schaaf, 1998) and perhaps also in the entorhinal cortex (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work, though the claim is qualified as 'perhaps'.

claim: Efficient coding implies that the threshold for perceiving a complex sensory cue should be set by its variance in the natural environment.
source: Behaviorally, efficient coding implies that the threshold for perceiving a complex sensory cue, which depends on the collective behavior of many cells in a cortical circuit, should be set by its variance in the natural environment.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the efficient coding framework.

claim: In conventional applications of efficient coding theory where sampling is abundant, high variance is predicted to be matched by high detection thresholds.
source: Specifically, in conventional applications of efficient coding theory where sampling is abundant, high variance is predicted to be matched by high detection thresholds.
evidence: This is a statement about established theory in the field.

claim: Texture perception occurs in a regime where sampling noise is the limiting factor.
source: The authors of Hermundstad et al., 2014 argued instead that texture perception occurs in a regime where sampling noise is the limiting factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hermundstad et al., 2014).

claim: In the sampling-limited regime, high variance should lead to a low detection threshold.
source: This leads to the opposite prediction (Tkacik et al., 2010; Doi and Lewicki, 2011; Hermundstad et al., 2014), namely that high variance should lead to a low detection threshold, summarized as variance is salience (Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The 'variance is salience' prediction holds for the visual detection of simple black-and-white binary textures.
source: Tests of this prediction in Tkacik et al., 2010; Hermundstad et al., 2014 showed that it holds for the visual detection of simple black-and-white binary textures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Binary textures do not capture many perceptually-salient properties of natural scenes.
source: These binary textures, while informative about visual sensitivity, are a highly restricted set and do not capture many perceptually-salient properties of natural scenes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of binary representations compared to natural scenes.

claim: Imposing translation symmetry on four binary checks leads to a 10-dimensional space of textures.
source: Imposing translation symmetry constrains these 16 parameters, leading to a 10-dimensional space of textures (Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and mathematical reasoning.

claim: The 'variance is salience' hypothesis qualitatively predicts that directions corresponding to two-point correlations will be most perceptually salient.
source: In particular, the 'variance is salience' hypothesis qualitatively predicts that directions corresponding to two-point correlations will be most perceptually salient
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the efficient coding framework.

claim: The 'variance is salience' hypothesis quantitatively predicts detection thresholds in different directions of the salient part of the texture space.
source: it quantitatively predicts detection thresholds in different directions of this salient part of the texture space
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that is tested against experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Predicted thresholds match psychophysical measurements with detailed agreement.
source: we found detailed agreement with the theory
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements.

claim: Human behavior reflects the relative informativeness of natural visual textures.
source: we show that human behavior not only reflects the relative informativeness of natural visual textures
evidence: This claim is supported by the psychophysical data showing correlation with natural scene statistics.

claim: Human behavior parallels known invariances in natural scenes.
source: we show that human behavior not only reflects the relative informativeness of natural visual textures, but it also parallels known invariances in natural scenes
evidence: This claim is supported by the symmetry analysis comparing natural images and psychophysical measurements.

claim: Natural scenes have a notable asymmetry between bright and dark.
source: Natural scenes also have a notable, previously studied, asymmetry between bright and dark (Ratliff et al., 2010; Tkacik et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The bright-dark asymmetry is reflected in the anatomy and physiology of visual circuits.
source: Natural scenes also have a notable, previously studied, asymmetry between bright and dark (Ratliff et al., 2010; Tkacik et al., 2010) which is reflected in the anatomy and physiology of visual circuits, and in visual behavior (Ratliff et al., 2010; Tkacik et al., 2010; Zemon et al., 1988; Chubb et al., 2004; Jin et al., 2008; Komban et al., 2014; Kremkow et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The bright-dark asymmetry is rooted in the lognormal distribution and spatial correlation structure of light intensities in natural scenes.
source: The asymmetry is rooted ultimately in the lognormal distribution and spatial correlation structure of light intensities in natural scenes (Ratliff et al., 2010; Tkačik et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ternarization procedure further diminishes the dark-light asymmetry.
source: The ternarization procedure that we then employ further diminishes the asymmetry
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the effects of the preprocessing steps.

claim: Translation invariance constrains the 81 probabilities, reducing the number of independent statistics.
source: However, translation invariance constrains these 81 probabilities, reducing the number of independent statistics and thus the dimension of the texture space.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference based on symmetry constraints.

claim: Check intensities can take three values (0, 1, or 2, for black, gray, or white).
source: Check intensities can take three values (0, 1, or 2, for black, gray, or white)
evidence: This is a definition of the encoding scheme used in the study.

claim: The frequencies of occurrence of the three intensity values must add to one, leaving two free parameters.
source: the corresponding frequencies of occurrence must add to one, leaving two free parameters
evidence: This is a mathematical constraint from probability theory.

claim: Translation invariance in natural images means the luminance histograms at each location within the glider must be the same.
source: However, because of translation invariance in natural images, the luminance histograms at each location must be the same, leaving only two independent dimensions of texture space from the single-check statistics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the symmetry properties of natural images.

claim: There are four ways to position pairs of checks within the glider, each with a different orientation.
source: Taking into account translation invariance, there are four ways to position these pairs (Figure 1B), each with a different orientation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and is a consequence of the geometric arrangement.

claim: The 8 second-order planes constitute 16 independent dimensions of the texture space.
source: These 8 planes constitute 16 independent dimensions of the texture space, in addition to the two dimensions needed to capture the histogram statistics at individual locations.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of having 8 planes with 2 independent coordinates each.

claim: For each 3-check glider position, eight parameters are needed to describe their occurrence frequencies, once first- and second-order statistics have been fixed.
source: for each of these positions, eight parameters are needed to describe their occurrence frequencies, once the first- and second-order statistics have been fixed
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the combinatorics and constraints.

claim: For configurations of all four checks, 16 parameters are required, once first-, second-, and third-order parameters are fixed.
source: For configurations of all four checks, 16 parameters are required, once first-, second-, and third-order parameters are fixed.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the combinatorics and constraints.

claim: The texture generation algorithm uses a Markov process designed to sample from a maximum-entropy distribution.
source: we randomly populate entries of the first row and/or column of the texture patch, and we then sequentially fill the rest of the entries in the patch using a Markov process that is designed to sample from a maximum-entropy distribution in which some of the texture coordinates are fixed
evidence: This is a methodological description of the texture synthesis algorithm.

claim: Natural images have much higher variance in the second-order coordinate planes than in the third- and fourth-order planes.
source: We found that natural images have much higher variance in the second-order coordinate planes than in the third- and fourth-order planes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the natural image analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Textures exhibiting variability in the second-order planes would be most salient to observers.
source: This predicted that textures exhibiting variability in the second-order planes would be most salient to observers
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the 'variance is salience' hypothesis and the natural image statistics.

claim: Predicted detection thresholds were computed in four single and twenty-two mixed second-order coordinate planes.
source: Thus, we computed the predicted detection thresholds in four single and twenty-two mixed second-order coordinate planes
evidence: This is a methodological description of the analysis performed.

claim: A single overall scaling factor was chosen to best match the behavioral measurements.
source: we scaled this set of thresholds by a single overall scaling factor that was chosen to best match the behavioral measurements
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the predictions were fit to the data.

claim: Subjects were briefly shown an array in which a rectangular strip was defined by a texture difference.
source: Subjects were briefly shown an array in which a rectangular strip positioned near the left, right, top, or bottom edge was defined by a texture difference
evidence: This is a description of the psychophysical task.

claim: Structured patterns were constructed using the texture generation method, and unstructured patterns were generated by randomly drawing black, gray, or white checks with equal probability.
source: Structured patterns were constructed using the texture generation method described above, and unstructured patterns were generated by randomly and independently drawing black, gray, or white checks with equal probability.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the stimulus generation.

claim: The texture analysis procedure included a whitening step that removed long-range correlations in natural images.
source: The texture analysis procedure in Figure 3 included a whitening step that removed long-range correlations in natural images
evidence: This is a methodological description shown in Figure 3.

claim: During natural vision, dynamic stimuli engage fixational eye movements that whiten the visual input.
source: This is appropriate, because, during natural vision, dynamic stimuli engage fixational eye movements that whiten the visual input (Rucci and Victor, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Adaptive spatiotemporal receptive field processing did not by itself whiten the retinal output.
source: but in vitro experiments (Simmons et al., 2013 found that adaptive spatiotemporal receptive field processing did not by itself whiten the retinal output, but rather served to maintain a similar degree of correlation across stimulus conditions)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Short visual stimuli like 120 ms presentations should be pre-whitened to make up for the absence of fixational eye movements.
source: We infer from these studies that short visual stimuli like our 120 ms presentations should be pre-whitened, to make up for the absence of fixational eye movements that produce whitening in natural, continuous viewing conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies about fixational eye movements and retinal processing.

claim: Thresholds were obtained by finding the value of a texture coordinate for which the subjects' performance was halfway between chance and perfect.
source: Thresholds were obtained by finding the value of a texture coordinate for which the subjects' performance was halfway between chance and perfect (Figure 4B; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a methodological description shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Subjects were highly consistent in their relative sensitivity to different directions in texture space for the second-order planes.
source: For the second-order planes, subjects were highly consistent in their relative sensitivity to different directions in texture space, with a single scaling factor accounting for a majority of the inter-subject variability
evidence: This claim is supported by the psychophysical data analysis.

claim: Sensitivity in the third and fourth-order planes was low.
source: As predicted by the natural scene analysis, sensitivity in the third and fourth-order planes was low
evidence: This claim is supported by the psychophysical measurements.

claim: Detection thresholds could not be reliably measured in most directions beyond second order.
source: in fact, detection thresholds could not be reliably measured in most directions beyond second order
evidence: This claim is supported by the psychophysical measurements.

claim: Predicted detection thresholds were in excellent agreement with those measured experimentally.
source: Predicted detection thresholds were in excellent agreement with those measured experimentally (Figure 4C and Figure 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figures 4C and 5.

claim: The median absolute log error between predictions and measurements is about 0.13.
source: with a median absolute log error of about 0.13
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of the agreement between predictions and measurements.

claim: 50% of the measurements have relative errors below 13%.
source: Put differently, 50% of the measurements have relative errors below 13%, since in this regime, the log error is very well approximated by relative error
evidence: This is a restatement of the median absolute log error in terms of relative error.

claim: 95% of the 10,000 permutation samples exhibited median absolute log errors in the range [0.24, 0.31].
source: 95% of the 10,000 permutation samples exhibited median absolute log errors in the range [0.24, 0.31]
evidence: This is a result from the permutation test analysis.

claim: The comparison between theory and experiment was tested in 12 directions in each of 26 single and mixed planes, for a total of 311 different thresholds.
source: The comparison between theory and experiment was tested in 12 directions in each of 26 single and mixed planes, for a total of 311 different thresholds
evidence: This is a description of the scope of the experimental measurements.

claim: A single scaling factor was used to align the predictions and measurements.
source: a single scaling factor was used to align these two sets of measurements
evidence: This is a methodological description of the fitting procedure.

claim: The natural image predictions within each plane lie on an ellipse by construction.
source: the natural image predictions within each plane lie on an ellipse by construction
evidence: This is a consequence of the Gaussian model fit to the natural image distribution.

claim: The psychophysical thresholds are generally well-approximated by ellipses.
source: the psychophysical thresholds are measured independently at each point but are generally well-approximated by ellipses
evidence: This is an observation from the psychophysical data.

claim: Not all thresholds are accurately predicted from natural images.
source: However, not all thresholds are accurately predicted from natural images.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the predictions.

claim: Natural-image predictions tend to underestimate the threshold in the simple planes (median log prediction error −0.090).
source: Natural-image predictions tend to underestimate the threshold in the simple planes (median log prediction error −0.090)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about systematic discrepancies.

claim: Natural-image predictions tend to overestimate the threshold in mixed planes (median log prediction error +0.008).
source: and overestimate the threshold in mixed planes (median log prediction error +0.008)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about systematic discrepancies.

claim: In human observers, detection of simultaneously-present multiple correlations is disproportionally better than predicted from the detection thresholds for single correlations.
source: That is, in human observers, detection of simultaneously-present multiple correlations is disproportionally better than predicted from the detection thresholds for single correlations, to a mild degree
evidence: This is an interpretation of the systematic discrepancy between simple and mixed planes.

claim: The larger errors for sum-correlations may be a consequence of how modular arithmetic and gray-level discretization interact.
source: This may be a consequence of the way that modular arithmetic and gray-level discretization interact, leading to a kind of non-robustness of the sum-correlations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Sum-correlations are subject to the particular assignment of gray levels and modulus while difference-correlations rely on relationships that hold independent of these choices.
source: Thus, the sum-correlations are subject to the particular assignment of gray levels and modulus while the difference-correlations rely on relationships that hold independent of these choices.
evidence: This is an inference about why sum-correlations might be less robust.

claim: Natural-image predictions tend to underestimate the thresholds in directions with very low variance even while they match the thresholds in directions with high variance.
source: Independent of these trends, the natural-image predictions tend to underestimate the thresholds in directions with very low variance even while they match the thresholds in directions with high variance
evidence: This is an observation about systematic patterns in the prediction errors.

claim: The systematic discrepancies suggest the need to go beyond the linear efficient-coding model.
source: This suggests the need to go beyond the linear efficient-coding model employed here.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed systematic discrepancies.

claim: A weak power-law nonlinearity might be involved in the relationship between variance and threshold.
source: suggesting that a weak power-law nonlinearity might be involved
evidence: This is an inference from the fitted exponent being close to but not exactly 1.

claim: The modest systematic discrepancies indicate that the efficient-coding model has limitations.
source: In sum, the modest systematic discrepancies between the natural-image predictions and the measured thresholds indicate that the efficient-coding model has limitations
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed discrepancies.

claim: The observed mismatches can guide future studies that go beyond the efficient-coding model.
source: and the observed mismatches can guide future studies that go beyond this model
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: Adapting to increasingly precise environmental statistics must ultimately become infeasible due to insufficient sampling and growing computational cost.
source: adapting to increasingly precise environmental statistics must ultimately become infeasible, both because of insufficient sampling, and because of the growing computational cost required for adaptation
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the limits of efficient coding.

claim: The results are robust to modifications in the way image patches are ternarized.
source: modify the way in which we ternarize image patches
evidence: This claim is supported by the robustness analysis.

claim: The results are robust to analyzing different image datasets.
source: or analyze different image datasets (Figure 6A and Appendix 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 6A and Appendix 3.

claim: The larger mismatches with N=1 are attributed to artifacts from imperfect demosaicing of the camera's filter array output.
source: as expected from Hermundstad et al., 2014, a finding that we attribute to artifacts arising from imperfect demosaicing of the camera's filter array output.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation, with citation to prior work.

claim: Reflecting a texture around the vertical axis has no effect on second-order statistics in the binary case.
source: Binary texture coordinates (Hermundstad et al., 2014) are not affected by many of these symmetry transformations
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of binary textures, with citation to prior work.

claim: Psychophysical thresholds are unaffected when textures are flipped about the vertical axis.
source: predicting that psychophysical thresholds should also be unaffected when textures are flipped about the vertical axis. This is indeed the case (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the psychophysical measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The natural image distribution is symmetric under flips about the horizontal axis.
source: Similarly, the natural image distribution is symmetric under flips about the horizontal axis
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image analysis.

claim: The natural image distribution is symmetric under rotations by 90, 180, and 270 degrees.
source: and also under rotations by 90, 180, and 270 degrees
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image analysis.

claim: Perceptual invariances under rotations are borne out in the psychophysical data.
source: predicting perceptual invariances that are borne out in the psychophysical data (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is a finding from the psychophysical measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The symmetry of diagonal correlations was already observed in the binary analysis.
source: This fact was already observed in the binary analysis (Hermundstad et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: These symmetries were not guaranteed to exist for either natural images or human psychophysics.
source: It is important to note that these symmetries were not guaranteed to exist for either natural images or human psychophysics.
evidence: This is a statement emphasizing the non-trivial nature of the observed symmetries.

claim: Most of the textures used are not themselves invariant under rotations.
source: Most of the textures that we are using are not themselves invariant under rotations (see the examples from Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is an observation about the individual textures shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Invariances of predicted thresholds arise from symmetries in the overall shape of the distribution of natural textures.
source: This means that invariances of predicted thresholds arise from symmetries in the overall shape of the distribution of natural textures.
evidence: This is an inference about the origin of the observed invariances.

claim: The psychophysical thresholds are invariant under precisely those transformations that leave the natural image distribution unchanged.
source: The fact that the psychophysical thresholds are, in fact, invariant under precisely those transformations that leave the natural image distribution unchanged supports the idea that this is an adaptation to symmetries present in the natural visual world.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of symmetries in natural images and psychophysics.

claim: The psychophysical data show a bright/dark asymmetry.
source: Our psychophysical data also show a bright/dark asymmetry.
evidence: This is an observation from the psychophysical measurements.

claim: The threshold contour is not symmetric under the exchange of black and white checks.
source: For instance, in Figure 4C, the threshold contour is not symmetric under the exchange of black and white checks
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 4C.

claim: Bright-dark asymmetries lead to a wide distribution of relative changes in detection threshold upon the exchange of black and white.
source: Such bright-dark asymmetries lead to a wide distribution of relative changes in detection threshold upon the exchange of black and white (red violin plot in Figure 6B for the exch(B,W) transformation).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The natural image analysis does not show bright-dark asymmetry because of preprocessing.
source: Our natural image analysis does not show this asymmetry (blue violin plot in Figure 6B for the exch(B,W) transformation) because of our preprocessing
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and explained by the preprocessing steps.

claim: The bright-dark asymmetry rests on a skewed distribution of light intensities and a power-law spectrum of spatial correlations.
source: As observed in Ratliff et al., 2010, the bright-dark asymmetry rests on two main characteristics of natural images: a skewed distribution of light intensities such that the mean intensity is larger than the median, and a power-law spectrum of spatial correlations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ternarization step additionally reduces any remaining dark-bright asymmetry.
source: The final ternarization step additionally reduces any remaining dark-bright asymmetry, since we ensure that each of the three gray levels occurs in equal proportions in the preprocessed patches.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the ternarization step affects the bright-dark asymmetry.

claim: The efficient coding hypothesis posits that sensory systems are adapted to maximize information about natural sensory stimuli.
source: The efficient coding hypothesis posits that sensory systems are adapted to maximize information about natural sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement of the theoretical framework being tested.

claim: This work provided a rigorous quantitative test of the efficient coding hypothesis in the context of visual processing of textures in a regime dominated by sampling noise.
source: In this work, we provided a rigorous quantitative test of this hypothesis in the context of visual processing of textures in a regime dominated by sampling noise.
evidence: This is a summary of the contribution of the work.

claim: The study extended the analysis of binary texture perception to grayscale images.
source: To this end, we extended the study of binary texture perception to grayscale images that capture a broader range of correlations to which the brain could conceivably adapt.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological contribution.

claim: Psychophysical thresholds can be predicted in remarkable detail based on the statistics of natural scenes.
source: By separately analyzing the distribution of textures across an ensemble of natural images, we showed that psychophysical thresholds can be predicted in remarkable detail based on the statistics of natural scenes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Visually-guided behavior shows the same invariances as the distribution of natural textures.
source: By further exploiting symmetry transformations that have non-trivial effects on ternary (but not binary) texture statistics, we provided a novel test of efficient coding and therein demonstrated that visually-guided behavior shows the same invariances as the distribution of natural textures.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding about symmetries.

claim: This work strengthens and refines the idea that the brain is adapted to efficiently encode visual texture information.
source: Overall, this work strengthens and refines the idea that the brain is adapted to efficiently encode visual texture information.
evidence: This is a summary of the overall conclusion.

claim: The methodology can be used to address many hypotheses about visual perception.
source: The methodology developed here can be used to address many hypotheses about visual perception.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader applicability of the methods.

claim: The ability of neural systems to adapt to correlations must ultimately be limited because it becomes impossible to collect sufficient statistics.
source: However, the ability of neural systems to adapt to such correlations must ultimately be limited because, as texture complexity grows, it will eventually become impossible for the brain to collect sufficient statistics to determine optimal sensitivities.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the limits of adaptation.

claim: Adapting to complex correlations might not be worth the computational cost.
source: Even were it possible to accumulate these statistics, adapting to them might not be worth the computational cost of detecting and processing long-range correlations between many intensity values.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about cost-benefit tradeoffs.

claim: Understanding the limits of texture adaptation will teach us about the cost-benefit tradeoffs of efficient coding in sensory cortex.
source: Understanding the limits of texture adaptation will teach us about the cost-benefit tradeoffs of efficient coding in sensory cortex, in analogy with recently identified cost-benefit tradeoffs in optimal inference (Tavoni et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the implications for future research, with citation to related work.

claim: The predictions are in excellent agreement with the data in most cases.
source: And indeed, although our predictions are in excellent agreement with the data in most cases
evidence: This is a summary of the overall quality of the predictions.

claim: There are a few systematic differences that may be giving a glimpse of the limits of efficient coding.
source: we find a few systematic differences that may already be giving us a glimpse of these limits
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed discrepancies.

claim: Images were taken from the UPenn Natural Image Database.
source: Images were taken from the UPenn Natural Image Database (Tkačik et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation to the data source.

claim: Patches were filtered to remove the average pairwise correlation expected in natural images.
source: filtered the patches to remove the average pairwise correlation expected in natural images (van Hateren, 1992)
evidence: This is a methodological description with citation to prior work.

claim: Patches were ternarized to produce equal numbers of black, gray, and white checks.
source: and finally ternarized patches to produce equal numbers of black, gray, and white checks
evidence: This is a methodological description of the preprocessing.

claim: A two-Gaussian mixture model was fit to the texture distribution to separate in-focus from blurred patches.
source: Finally, to avoid biases due to blurring artifacts, we fit a two-Gaussian mixture model to the texture distribution and used this to separate in-focus from blurred patches (Figure 3B; Hermundstad et al., 2014; details in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological description shown in Figure 3B, with citation to prior work.

claim: Stimuli were presented on a mean-gray background for 120 ms.
source: Stimuli, as described above, were presented on a mean-gray background for 120 ms
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulus presentation.

claim: Stimuli were followed by a mask consisting of an array of i.i.d. checks, each half the size of the stimulus checks.
source: followed by a mask consisting of an array of i.i.d. checks, each half the size of the stimulus checks
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulus presentation.

claim: Viewing distance was 103 cm.
source: viewing distance was 103 cm
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental setup.

claim: The display device was an LCD monitor with a refresh rate of 100 Hz.
source: The display device was an LCD monitor with a refresh rate of 100 Hz
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental equipment.

claim: The monitor was calibrated with a photometer prior to each day of data collection.
source: The monitor was calibrated with a photometer prior to each day of data collection
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental procedure.

claim: The luminance of the gray checks was halfway between that of the black checks (<0.1) and white checks (23 cd/m2).
source: to ensure that the luminance of the gray checks was halfway between that of the black checks (<0.1) and white checks (23 cd/m2)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimulus calibration.

claim: Subjects were normal volunteers (three male, three female), ages 20 to 57.
source: Subjects were normal volunteers (three male, three female), ages 20 to 57
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All subjects had visual acuities, corrected if necessary, of 20/20 or better.
source: with visual acuities, corrected if necessary, of 20/20 or better
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: MC is an experienced psychophysical observer with thousands of hours of experience.
source: Of the six subjects, MC is an experienced psychophysical observer with thousands of hours of experience
evidence: This is a description of one of the participants.

claim: MC is an author.
source: MC is an author.
evidence: This is a disclosure about one of the participants.
